input.quote: 7.2 Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
input.rationale: Section 7.2 (p0026) conditions our right to engage another provider on first disclosing any more favourable third-party offer and matching it for Vendor. That is a disclose-and-match gate that functions as de facto exclusivity plus a most-favoured-customer commitment binding Customer: we cannot freely source elsewhere without giving Vendor a right of first refusal on price, and it is unlimited as to category, duration, and has no performance-based exit. It also directly contradicts Section 12.3 (p0044), in which Vendor acknowledges Customer has made no exclusivity or most-favoured-customer commitment, and Section 2.2's precedence ladder does not resolve an internal conflict within the Agreement. No other exclusivity provision binds Customer (the remaining "exclusive" references concern the non-exclusive licence, remedies, and jurisdiction). Preferred position is no exclusivity obligation on Customer, so we delete the clause; the fallback (narrow category, 12 months, automatic termination on missed service levels) is offered in the comment.

proposal.summary: Delete the disclose-and-match gate at § 7.2 that operates as de facto exclusivity on Customer.
proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have deleted the requirement to disclose and match competing offers before engaging another provider, because it operates as a de facto exclusivity and most-favoured-customer commitment on us and contradicts Section 12.3, under which we make no exclusivity or MFC commitment. If Cobalt needs some form of preference, we could consider a narrow arrangement limited to a defined service category for no more than twelve months that ends automatically on any missed service level or delivery date.
